node.label: Matthew Frye Jacobson
node.date_label: Whiteness of a Different Color (1998) · Barbarian Virtues (2000) · Roots Too (2006)
node.description: A historian of race, migration and political culture in the United States. His written PBS interview explains how distinctions among European immigrants were once treated as racial differences and later reconfigured as ethnicity. He connects those changing categories to arguments about fitness for citizenship and self-government. The entry treats racial classifications as historical objects, retains the distinctions between scholarly claims and the categories of historical actors, and does not certify every example in the unread monographs.

incident_edges.relationship: Historicizes shifting racial subdivisions within whiteness and their reconfiguration as ethnic differences.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Primary written interview, opening questions on race around 1900 and immigration. These are the historian’s arguments about changing classifications; quoted historical categories are not endorsed.

incident_edges.relationship: Connects racial classification with historical disputes about naturalization and fitness for self-government.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Primary answer on immigration and the 1790 naturalization framework, plus the discussion of later immigration debates. This is a particular historical interpretation, not current legal guidance or an influence arrow.

incident_edges.relationship: Uses Jacobson’s account of whiteness and credits his reading of the Impossible Subjects manuscript.
incident_edges.evidence_note: The 1999 article, p. 70 and note 9, explicitly attributes the formulation of a consanguine white race to Matthew Jacobson and identifies Whiteness of a Different Color (1998). The work identifies Matthew Frye Jacobson rather than a namesake. The reprinted acknowledgment, p. xvi, names him among readers of all or part of the penultimate draft. The conceptual and manuscript roles are consolidated here; his original book remains unread.
